drills.q: Explain mechanically why df.apply(func, axis=1) is slower than df.a + df.b, even though both are one line of code.
drills.a: apply calls a Python function once per row, and pandas has to assemble each row's values into a Series-like object per call, executing entirely in the Python interpreter. The vectorised form runs a single compiled NumPy loop over contiguous column memory with no per-row Python function-call overhead at all.

drills.q: A Series is created from [1, 2, None, 4]. What dtype does it get, and why?
drills.a: float64. NumPy's int64 has no bit pattern to represent a missing value, so pandas upcasts the entire column to float64 (which can represent NaN) the moment any value is missing — every value, including the non-missing ones, becomes a float.

drills.q: Given df.groupby('team')['score'].transform('mean'), what shape does the result have relative to the input, and how does that differ from .agg('mean')?
drills.a: transform returns a result with the SAME shape (same number of rows) as the input, broadcasting each group's mean back to every row belonging to that group. agg('mean') instead collapses each group to one row, returning one value per group, not per original row.

drills.q: You need, for each row, its deviation from its group's mean (score - group_mean). Write this using transform, and explain why agg alone can't do it in one step.
drills.a: df['score'] - df.groupby('team')['score'].transform('mean'). agg alone produces one row per group, so subtracting it from the original per-row score requires re-aligning the per-group value back onto every original row — which is exactly the broadcast transform performs internally; with agg alone you'd need a separate merge back onto the original frame on the grouping key.

drills.q: What does merge(df1, df2, on='key', validate='one_to_one') check, and what happens if the check fails?
drills.a: It verifies that 'key' is unique in BOTH df1 and df2 before performing the merge. If either side has duplicate keys, it raises MergeError immediately, before any rows are silently fanned out by the merge.

drills.q: Prior to pandas 3.0, what made SettingWithCopyWarning ambiguous rather than a clear error, and what specifically changed in pandas 3.0 (January 2026)?
drills.a: Whether df[mask] returned a view (sharing memory with the original) or an independent copy was an undocumented implementation detail depending on internal memory layout, so the same-looking chained assignment code could silently mutate the original in one case and do nothing in another. Pandas 3.0 made Copy-on-Write the only mode — every operation behaves as an independent copy by contract — removed SettingWithCopyWarning entirely, and made chained assignment raise an explicit error instead of warning.

drills.q: Design a pandas approach to expand a table of (contract_id, start_date, end_date) rows into one row per (contract_id, month) for every month the range spans. Name the specific edge case that requires a guard.
drills.a: For each row, generate pd.date_range(start_date, end_date, freq='MS').tolist() to get the list of month-start timestamps in range, store it in a column, then call df.explode() on that column to turn each row's list into separate rows, duplicating the other columns. The edge case: a row whose start and end fall within the same calendar month produces zero month-start boundaries strictly between them, giving an empty list — without a fallback (e.g. defaulting to [start_date.replace(day=1)]), that row silently disappears entirely under explode.

drills.q: Give the SQL equivalent of the date-range-to-month-rows expansion, in both a generate_series form and a calendar-table form, and state when you'd prefer each.
drills.a: generate_series form (Postgres/DuckDB): CROSS JOIN LATERAL generate_series(date_trunc('month', start_date), date_trunc('month', end_date), interval '1 month') per contract row — terser, no auxiliary table, but engine-specific. Calendar-table form: JOIN a pre-populated date-dimension table ON cal.month BETWEEN date_trunc('month', start_date) AND date_trunc('month', end_date) — more portable across engines lacking generate_series (e.g. older SQL Server), common in data warehouses that already maintain such a table.

drills.q: Explain why rolling(window=7) can give a misleading answer on a datetime-indexed daily series that has a gap (a missing day), and how to fix it.
drills.a: By default rolling windows by a fixed number of ROWS, not by elapsed calendar time. If there's a gap in the index, 'the last 7 rows' actually spans more than 7 calendar days, silently including data further back in time than a caller expecting a 7-day window would assume. Fix: use a time-based window string, rolling('7D'), which pandas resolves against the actual datetime index rather than row count, correctly handling gaps.

drills.q: A groupby aggregation over 100 million rows is taking over 100 seconds (or exhausting memory) in pandas. Diagnose two likely contributing factors and name the tools you'd consider switching to, with the rough scale threshold that justifies each.
drills.a: Likely factors: pandas executes single-threaded with no query optimizer, and grouping/aggregating with a custom Python callable (rather than a named/vectorised function) forces a per-group Python callback instead of a compiled path. Above roughly 1-5GB or needing multi-core execution, switch to Polars (multi-threaded by default, lazy query optimization) — the same groupby often finishes in well under 30 seconds there. For SQL-shaped aggregation directly over files larger than RAM without a separate warehouse, DuckDB is the better fit.

drills.q: When does converting a string column to category dtype NOT help, and why, especially considering pandas 3.0's new default string dtype?
drills.a: It doesn't help on high-cardinality columns (mostly-unique values like UUIDs or free text) — the codes array approaches the same size as just storing the values directly, plus the overhead of maintaining the category mapping. Pandas 3.0's PyArrow-backed default string dtype is already meaningfully more memory-efficient than the old object dtype, narrowing the gap category used to close, though category still wins decisively for genuinely low-cardinality columns since it avoids storing repeated string content at all.
